statement: For random variables (or vectors) X, Y and conditioning variable Z, X is conditionally independent of Y given Z, written X⊥⊥Y∣Z, iff P(X,Y∣Z) = P(X∣Z)P(Y∣Z) — i.e., once Z is known, learning Y gives no further information about X (informally: an observation is irrelevant or redundant to a hypothesis once the conditioning information is known).

symbols.meaning: random variable or vector (the hypothesis/quantity of interest)
random variable or vector (the candidate observation)
conditioning random variable or vector (known information)
joint probability (or density/CDF) of X and Y given Z

properties.why: the defining equation P(X,Y∣Z)=P(X∣Z)P(Y∣Z) is unchanged by swapping X and Y

properties.property: Decomposition: X⊥⊥Y∣Z ⇒ h(X)⊥⊥Y∣Z for any function h; in particular (X,W)⊥⊥Y∣Z ⇒ X⊥⊥Y∣Z and X⊥⊥(Y,W)∣Z ⇒ X⊥⊥Y∣Z
properties.why: summing the joint conditional over X-values mapping to a fixed h(X)=a preserves the product form

properties.property: Weak union: X⊥⊥Y∣Z ⇒ X⊥⊥Y∣(Z,h(X)) for any function h; special cases X⊥⊥(Y,W)∣Z ⇒ X⊥⊥Y∣(Z,W) and (X,W)⊥⊥Y∣Z ⇒ X⊥⊥Y∣(Z,W)
properties.why: conditioning further on a function of X does not reintroduce dependence once X⊥⊥Y∣Z already holds
Pr(X∣A,B)=Pr(X∣B)=Pr(X) chains the two given equalities into joint independence of X from (A,B)

properties.property: Intersection (strictly positive distributions only): (X⊥⊥Y∣Z,W and X⊥⊥W∣Z,Y) ⇒ X⊥⊥(W,Y)∣Z
properties.why: the two hypotheses force P(X∣Z,Y)=P(X∣Z,W), and the law of total probability over W then collapses P(X∣Z) to P(X∣Z,Y)

assumptions.assumption: The intersection property requires the joint probability distribution to be strictly positive.
assumptions.breaks_when: some outcome has zero probability, e.g. deterministic constraints among variables

failure_modes.mode: Assuming marginal independence (X⊥⊥Y) implies conditional independence (X⊥⊥Y∣Z), or vice versa
failure_modes.signature: independence claim holds unconditionally but is used inside a conditioned model (or vice versa) without re-derivation
failure_modes.cause: conditional independence and marginal independence are logically distinct relations; neither implies the other in general

failure_modes.mode: Applying the Intersection rule to a distribution with zero-probability events
failure_modes.signature: derived independence conclusion contradicts direct calculation
failure_modes.cause: Intersection's proof relies on strict positivity to divide by P(W=w∣Z) terms via the law of total probability
